claims.text: The protective behavior of pre-exposure Q235 steel is governed by its native iron-oxide film.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel naturally has a thin iron-oxide passive layer.
At room temperature, the native oxide film remains intact and slows corrosion.
The native Fe-oxide layer limits ion transfer at room temperature.
Aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C thermally destabilizes the native oxide film on Q235 steel.
At high temperature, the native oxide transforms into porous, non-protective phases or dissolves into the salt.
Destabilization of the oxide film causes spallation.
Transformation or dissolution of the oxide exposes fresh metal and accelerates oxidation and degradation.
Under high-temperature salt exposure, native-oxide Q235 specimens will exhibit measurable mass loss and a higher oxidation rate than under room-temperature exposure.
Under high-temperature salt exposure, native-oxide Q235 specimens will develop spalled or porous oxide structures.
A controlled, uniform, stabilized passivation film may resist high-temperature degradation better than the native Q235 oxide.
The proposed mechanism applies to untreated Q235 steel carrying its native oxide.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when Q235 steel has a deliberately engineered, more stable passivation layer.
Q235 steel has insufficient alloying additions to form durable passivation films comparable to more highly alloyed steels.
More highly alloyed steels and engineered coatings may exhibit corrosion behavior governed by mechanisms other than native iron-oxide instability.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes specimens 'with and without' the native oxide, but the nominally oxide-free specimens are re-oxidized or given a stabilized replacement film. Thus, the actual comparison is native oxide versus engineered oxide, not oxide-present versus oxide-absent.
